title: API Gateway & Reverse Proxies
intro: An API Gateway acts as the single entry point for client applications, orchestrating routing, protocol translation, authentication, and cross-cutting security.
objectives: Implement centralized authentication, TLS termination, and distributed rate limiting.
Apply the Backend-For-Frontend (BFF) architectural pattern for mobile and web clients.
Configure canary traffic splitting and circuit-breaking at the edge tier.
body:
### Responsibilities of an API Gateway
In a microservices architecture, exposing dozens of internal services directly to mobile or web clients creates tight coupling, security vulnerabilities, and network chattiness. An API Gateway encapsulates internal microservice topology:
- **Security**: Terminating TLS, validating OAuth2 / JWT bearer tokens, and blocking malicious payloads.
- **Rate Limiting**: Enforcing token-bucket throttles by IP or API key before requests touch compute tiers.
- **Protocol Translation**: Translating external REST/JSON HTTP requests into high-speed internal gRPC Protobuf calls.
- **Canary Routing**: Shifting 5% of user traffic to experimental service versions using header rules.
keyIdea: Centralize cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, telemetry) at the API Gateway so microservices can focus purely on business logic.

concepts.title: Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)
concepts.body: Dedicated lightweight gateways tailored for specific client formats (e.g. mobile BFF optimizing payload size vs desktop web BFF).

concepts.title: Request Aggregation
concepts.body: The gateway calls multiple downstream microservices in parallel and merges the responses into a single combined payload for mobile clients.

examples: Kong / Envoy API Gateway validating JWTs and enforcing Redis rate limits.

quiz.prompt: What architectural pattern creates distinct gateway instances tailored specifically for web vs mobile clients?
quiz.explanation: BFF creates client-specific gateways so mobile payloads can be aggressively trimmed for cellular networks.
